title: Own the application shell as an application composition
decision: How to frame the top level of a Fluent UI React v9 application
appliesWhen: A React app renders more than one screen.
exceptions: A single-screen prototype may render one page without a persistent shell.
notApplicableWhen: The app is embedded inside an existing host frame that owns navigation.
instruction: Compose the whole application inside a FluentProvider and build the shell navigation yourself from Nav, Toolbar, and layout primitives, because v9 exports no shell component.
rationale: Fluent owns presentational components, not the application frame. Treating a shell as a library API leads to invented props and unsupported upgrades.

componentMapping.note: The app shell combines FluentProvider, Nav, and layout primitives; no single v9 export provides it.

layoutConsequences: The shell reserves a bounded navigation column and a flexible content column, so page content never controls the global frame.
responsiveConsequences: Below the project's narrow breakpoint the navigation column collapses to a drawer or an overlay nav rather than shrinking to unreadable widths.
accessibilityImplications: The shell provides the banner and navigation landmarks, and keeps one main landmark for the routed content.
stateImplications: The shell owns which navigation region is expanded or open; route state lives in the application router.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: Fluent UI React ships an official application-shell component.

positiveExample: A root FluentProvider wraps an application-defined Nav and a routed content outlet.
antiPattern: Importing an `AppShell` component from @fluentui/react-components and passing width props to it.
verificationMethod: check-facts rejects an `AppShell` export, and the fixture shell renders with the expected landmarks under axe.

title: Use Nav for the primary hierarchy and Breadcrumb for position
decision: How to present primary navigation and the current location
appliesWhen: The application has a stable hierarchy of destinations.
exceptions: A single-destination tool may show no navigation region at all.
notApplicableWhen: Navigation is provided by the host environment rather than the app.
instruction: Render the primary destinations with Nav and its item parts, and render the current position with Breadcrumb, because routing itself stays application-owned.
rationale: Nav supplies the disclosure and selection behavior for a hierarchy; Breadcrumb expresses position. Neither one performs routing, so the app must bind them to its router.
layoutConsequences: Navigation occupies one consistent region across screens so destinations do not shift between pages.
responsiveConsequences: At narrow widths the same Nav content moves into NavDrawer instead of being clipped.
accessibilityImplications: Navigation must expose a navigation landmark and mark the current destination, so assistive technology can report both structure and position.
stateImplications: The application selects the active item to match the route and owns whether categories are expanded.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: Nav changes its selection or disclosure contract in a breaking release.

positiveExample: NavItem selection is derived from the active route, and Breadcrumb trails the route segments.
antiPattern: Adding `href` to Nav items and expecting the component to change the route without application handling.
verificationMethod: A test asserts that the active route marks exactly one navigation item as current.

title: Give each page one heading that names its task
decision: How to establish page identity and hierarchy
appliesWhen: A routed screen renders any content.
notApplicableWhen: The screen is a transient overlay that inherits the underlying page heading.
instruction: Place a single top-level heading that names the screen's task at the start of the content region, and use lower heading levels only for structure beneath it.
rationale: A single heading gives the page a landmark and lets assistive technology announce where the user is; competing top-level headings break that contract.
layoutConsequences: The heading anchors the content region and sets the vertical rhythm for everything below it.
responsiveConsequences: The heading keeps its semantic level while its rendered size may step down at narrow widths.
accessibilityImplications: Exactly one first-level heading per screen preserves a usable document outline for screen-reader navigation.
stateImplications: The heading text follows the loaded record or task and updates when that subject changes.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The component offers a heading component that manages document outline automatically.

positiveExample: A detail page begins with one Title1 naming the record, followed by Subtitle1 section headings.
antiPattern: Rendering two Title1 elements, or using heading components purely to reach a visual size.
verificationMethod: An automated axe check reports no heading-order violation on the rendered page.

title: Keep one primary action and move the rest into a toolbar
decision: How to place page-level commands
appliesWhen: A screen offers commands that act on the whole screen or record.
exceptions: A confirmation screen may present two equally weighted actions when the choice is genuinely binary.
notApplicableWhen: The screen is read-only and offers no commands.
instruction: Reserve one visually primary action for the screen and place additional page commands in a Toolbar, moving overflow actions into a menu.
rationale: One primary action per view keeps the intended next step obvious and prevents a wall of equally weighted buttons.
layoutConsequences: Commands sit in a consistent region so users learn where actions live across screens.
responsiveConsequences: At narrow widths the toolbar overflows into a menu instead of wrapping into many rows.
accessibilityImplications: Toolbar buttons need accessible names, and overflow menus must be operable by keyboard with visible focus.
stateImplications: The application owns command enablement, including disabled states while a request is pending.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: Product research shows a workflow needs multiple equally weighted primary actions.

positiveExample: A Save button is the primary action, while Export and Delete live in a toolbar menu.
antiPattern: Presenting five solid buttons with equal emphasis in the page header.
verificationMethod: The fixture asserts one primary-styled action per screen and a keyboard-reachable overflow menu.

title: Bind every input to a visible label and helper text
decision: How to associate labels, help, and errors with inputs
appliesWhen: A form presents an editable control.
exceptions: A search box may rely on a placeholder only when the control is paired with a visible label elsewhere in the same region.
notApplicableWhen: The control is not an input and accepts no user text.
instruction: Wrap each control in a Field that provides a visible label, and place help or error text through the Field's message slot rather than beside it.
rationale: A programmatic label is required for assistive technology, and placing messages through Field keeps the announcement tied to the input.
layoutConsequences: Field reserves space for the label and message so validation does not shift the surrounding layout unexpectedly.
responsiveConsequences: Labels stay adjacent to their controls at narrow widths instead of floating to a separate column.
accessibilityImplications: The label must be programmatically associated, and an error message must be announced when it appears.
stateImplications: The application owns the value, the validation state, and the message text passed to Field.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The platform guarantees labeling for a control without a Field wrapper.

positiveExample: Each Field supplies a text label and a validationMessage that the input references.
antiPattern: Rendering a bare Input with only a placeholder and no label element.
verificationMethod: A test asserts every rendered input resolves an accessible name, and axe reports no label violation.

title: Validate on blur and submit, and after the user has entered a value
decision: When validation feedback should appear
appliesWhen: A field has constraints that can fail.
exceptions: Real-time validation is appropriate when the constraint is about availability, such as a duplicate name check.
notApplicableWhen: The field has no constraints.
instruction: Show a field error after the user leaves the field or submits the form, and never before the user has entered a value, so the form does not scold an untouched field.
rationale: Validating an untouched field reports an error the user has not had a chance to fix, which is noisy and erodes trust.
layoutConsequences: Reserving message space prevents the form from jumping when an error appears.
responsiveConsequences: Error text wraps beneath the field on narrow screens rather than overflowing.
accessibilityImplications: The error must be programmatically associated with the input and announced without moving focus unexpectedly.
stateImplications: The application tracks touched, dirty, and submitted state to decide when a message is shown.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: User testing shows a specific constraint needs immediate feedback.

positiveExample: A required email field shows its error only after blur.
antiPattern: Showing a red error on every field the moment the form renders.
verificationMethod: A test asserts no error is shown before interaction and that an invalid value reports once on blur.

title: Default forms to a single column and group related fields
decision: How to lay out a form's fields
appliesWhen: A form presents more than a few fields.
exceptions: Short, tightly related pairs such as city and region may share one row.
notApplicableWhen: The form has a single field.
instruction: Lay fields out in one column by default and group related fields under a shared heading, because a single reading path is easier to follow and to complete.
rationale: Multiple columns create an ambiguous reading order and make long forms harder to scan, especially for users of magnifiers.
layoutConsequences: A single column sets one consistent alignment and spacing rhythm down the form.
responsiveConsequences: A single column survives narrow widths without reflowing into a different reading order.
accessibilityImplications: Grouped fields should be introduced by a heading or fieldset so their relationship is announced.
stateImplications: Grouping is presentational; each field keeps its own value and validation state.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The form is a dense data-entry grid where comparison across columns is the primary task.

positiveExample: A record editor stacks fields vertically and groups them under Account and Contact headings.
antiPattern: A three-column field grid whose tab order jumps across the page.
verificationMethod: The fixture form renders one field per row at narrow widths with an unchanged tab order.

title: Use a dialog for a short, focused decision
decision: When to interrupt with a modal dialog
appliesWhen: The user must confirm a decision or complete a short task before continuing.
exceptions: A destructive confirmation may use the alert variant so the backdrop does not dismiss it.
notApplicableWhen: The task is long or needs access to the underlying page.
instruction: Place a short, self-contained decision in a Dialog with a title and explicit action buttons, so the interaction stays bounded and easy to dismiss.
rationale: Dialogs are interruptive by design; a bounded task with a title and clear actions keeps the interruption predictable.
layoutConsequences: The dialog is a separate surface, so the page beneath keeps its layout and scroll position.
responsiveConsequences: At narrow widths the surface fits the viewport and its content scrolls instead of overflowing.
accessibilityImplications: The dialog must have a title, trap focus while open, and return focus to the trigger on close.
stateImplications: The application owns the open state and any pending action, including disabling actions while work is in progress.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The dialog primitive changes its focus or dismissal contract.

positiveExample: A delete action opens a Dialog titled with the record name and Cancel and Delete actions.
antiPattern: A dialog with no title that closes on any backdrop click while a request is pending.
verificationMethod: A test asserts focus enters the dialog on open and returns to the trigger on close.

title: Prefer a drawer over a dialog for a longer contextual edit
decision: How to present a contextual edit that does not deserve a full page
appliesWhen: The user edits a short group of fields in the context of a list or detail page.
exceptions: A very short confirmation still belongs in a dialog.
notApplicableWhen: The edit needs many steps or a large amount of content.
instruction: Use a Drawer for a contextual edit that keeps the underlying context visible, and confirm before discarding unsaved changes when the drawer closes.
rationale: A drawer allows a modest amount of focused work without replacing the whole page, while preserving the sense of context.
layoutConsequences: The drawer slides over part of the page, so the list or record behind it keeps its position.
responsiveConsequences: At narrow widths the drawer can occupy the full width without becoming a separate route.
accessibilityImplications: The drawer needs a labeled title, a keyboard path to close, and focus returned to the invoking control.
stateImplications: The application owns dirty state and decides whether closing requires confirmation.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The edit grows beyond a small, single-purpose field group.

positiveExample: Editing a row's status opens a drawer with a small Field set and a dirty-state guard on close.
antiPattern: Opening a full drawer to edit one field, or losing typed values when the drawer is dismissed.
verificationMethod: A test asserts the drawer returns focus to its trigger and prompts before discarding a changed value.

title: Choose DataGrid when columns control layout and Table when the DOM table matters
decision: How to choose between DataGrid and Table for tabular data
appliesWhen: The screen presents rows and columns of data.
exceptions: A simple, static comparison with no sorting or selection can use the plain Table.
notApplicableWhen: The data is not tabular.
instruction: Use DataGrid when the layout must be controlled by column definitions and keyboard grid behavior is required, and use Table when a native table structure is the goal.
rationale: The two components make different promises: DataGrid gives controlled columns and a grid interaction model, while Table renders a semantic DOM table.
layoutConsequences: DataGrid columns can be sized and prioritized; a Table lays itself out from its content.
responsiveConsequences: A grid with many columns needs an explicit narrow-width strategy, such as hiding low-priority columns or allowing horizontal scroll within a labeled region.
accessibilityImplications: DataGrid follows the grid keyboard model, so arrow keys move between cells; Table exposes native table semantics without that keyboard contract.
stateImplications: Sort, filter, and selection state are owned by the application and passed back through column definitions or props.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: A first-party DataGrid usage guide changes the recommended interaction model.

positiveExample: A sortable, selectable list uses DataGrid with typed column definitions.
antiPattern: Nesting interactive buttons inside a DataGrid cell while also using single-click row activation.
verificationMethod: The fixture list page renders a DataGrid and passes axe grid checks and a keyboard navigation test.

title: State whether sorting, filtering, and paging run locally or on the server
decision: Where collection operations execute
appliesWhen: A collection can be sorted, filtered, or paged.
notApplicableWhen: The collection is small, fully loaded, and not sortable or filterable.
instruction: Decide explicitly whether each collection operation runs on loaded rows or on the server, and pass the resulting state into the grid so the component does not imply a data source it does not have.
rationale: The component does not fetch or process data; leaving the choice implicit leads to a grid that appears to sort a full collection while only rearranging the current page.
layoutConsequences: Server-side paging needs room for a pager and a result count near the grid.
responsiveConsequences: The pager collapses to a compact control at narrow widths rather than wrapping awkwardly.
accessibilityImplications: When results change asynchronously, the grid or a status region must announce the update and any pending state.
stateImplications: The application owns page, sort, filter, and loading state and re-fetches when they change.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: A first-party data-fetching convenience API makes the ownership explicit.

positiveExample: A server-paged grid re-queries on sort change and shows a Spinner in the grid region while loading.
antiPattern: Sorting only the current page of a server-paged collection and presenting it as a full sort.
verificationMethod: A fixture test changes the sort and asserts a new request is issued for server-mode grids.

title: State whether a selection applies to loaded rows or to all matching results
decision: The scope of a bulk selection
appliesWhen: A collection supports multi-row selection and bulk actions.
notApplicableWhen: The collection supports only single-row actions.
instruction: Make the selection scope explicit to the user, and when a bulk action can apply to all matching results rather than only the loaded page, offer that choice deliberately.
rationale: A header checkbox that silently means only the current page causes destructive mistakes when a bulk action follows.
layoutConsequences: The selection state and any select-all scope control belong next to the grid header, not in a distant toolbar.
responsiveConsequences: The scope choice must remain reachable at narrow widths, for example inside an overflow menu.
accessibilityImplications: Selection changes must be announced, and the scope control needs an accessible name that states what it selects.
stateImplications: The application tracks selected ids separately from the loaded page and owns the meaning of select-all.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The grid component provides a first-class all-matching selection mode.

positiveExample: The header control explicitly offers Select page and Select all matching results.
antiPattern: A header checkbox that selects only visible rows while a bulk delete labels it Select all.
verificationMethod: A test asserts the bulk action receives the ids for the currently chosen scope.

title: Do not hide task-required fields inside a collapsed section
decision: What may be placed inside disclosure such as an accordion
appliesWhen: A surface uses an accordion or another collapsed disclosure.
notApplicableWhen: The surface has no collapsible regions.
instruction: Keep fields that the task requires visible or clearly summarized, and reserve collapsed sections for genuinely optional or advanced content.
rationale: Collapsed content is easy to miss, and a validation error inside a closed section can block submission with no visible cause.
layoutConsequences: Optional sections sit after the required content so the required path is the visible path.
responsiveConsequences: Disclosure works the same at narrow widths; collapsing does not become the only way to fit content.
accessibilityImplications: The header must expose expanded state, and an error inside a collapsed section must be surfaced outside it as well.
stateImplications: The application tracks expanded sections and must open a section that contains a blocking error.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: Validation is guaranteed to surface outside collapsed regions by the platform.

positiveExample: Advanced connection settings collapse, while required name and owner fields stay visible.
antiPattern: Hiding a required field in a closed Advanced section and failing submission with no visible error.
verificationMethod: A test asserts that a validation error inside a collapsed section opens the section and is announced.

title: Use tabs for peer views and not for sequential steps
decision: When to switch content with tabs
appliesWhen: A region presents several peer views of the same subject.
exceptions: A wizard may use a custom step indicator rather than tabs.
notApplicableWhen: The views are sequential steps of one task.
instruction: Use TabList to switch between peer views of the same record, and keep sequential task steps out of tabs so users are not misled about order.
rationale: Tabs imply parallel alternatives; using them for ordered steps hides the intended sequence and makes progress hard to read.
layoutConsequences: Tabs stay in one region and replace only that region, leaving the surrounding page stable.
responsiveConsequences: At narrow widths overflow tabs move into a menu or become a Select rather than scrolling out of reach.
accessibilityImplications: Tabs follow the tablist keyboard model, and the selected tab must be programmatically associated with its panel.
stateImplications: The application owns the selected tab and may reflect it in the route or query string.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The design uses tabs purely as visual navigation with no sequential meaning.

positiveExample: Overview, Members, and Settings are peer tabs on a record detail page.
antiPattern: Modeling a three-step checkout as three tabs without any order or progress signal.
verificationMethod: A test asserts that the selected tab controls the visible panel and is operable by arrow keys.

title: Choose persistence by urgency: MessageBar for durable, Toast for transient
decision: How to deliver status and feedback
appliesWhen: The application reports the result of an action or a persistent condition.
exceptions: A toast may carry an action when the result is transient and non-critical.
notApplicableWhen: There is no status to report.
instruction: Place conditions the user must be able to read later in a MessageBar, and place short-lived confirmations in a Toast, because the two differ in persistence and urgency.
rationale: A toast disappears and cannot be re-read, so treating it as the only record of a failure loses information the user needs.
layoutConsequences: A durable message occupies space in the page; a toast floats above it without displacing content.
responsiveConsequences: Toasts stack and fit the viewport at narrow widths, and durable messages wrap in place.
accessibilityImplications: Urgent messages need an appropriate live-region politeness, and a toast must remain long enough to read and be dismissible.
stateImplications: The application owns which condition is current and when a transient notice is removed.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The design adds a persistent notification center that changes the default.

positiveExample: A failed save shows a MessageBar that stays until resolved, while a successful copy shows a toast.
antiPattern: Reporting a failed save only with a toast that fades after a few seconds.
verificationMethod: A test asserts the failure state remains present in the DOM after the toast duration elapses.

title: Design explicit loading, empty, search-empty, and error states
decision: What a data region shows when it has no content to show
appliesWhen: A region loads or lists data.
notApplicableWhen: The region renders static content that never loads.
instruction: Provide a distinct state for loading, for genuinely empty data, for an empty search result, and for a failed load, so the user can tell the difference and knows what to do next.
rationale: A blank region is ambiguous: the user cannot tell whether the data is loading, absent, filtered out, or failed.
layoutConsequences: Each state reserves the region's space so the page does not collapse or jump between states.
responsiveConsequences: State messages and illustrations scale down without truncating the explanation or the recovery action.
accessibilityImplications: Loading must be announced without trapping focus, and errors must be announced and paired with a recovery action.
stateImplications: The application owns a distinct status value for each state rather than inferring it from an empty array.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: A shared data-region component centralizes these states.

positiveExample: The list shows skeletons while loading, a FilterBar-aware empty message for no matches, and a retry action on failure.
antiPattern: Rendering the same No results text for an empty dataset and for a failed request.
verificationMethod: Fixture tests drive each state and assert a distinct, announced message with a recovery action where relevant.

title: Style through the two-layer token model, not hard-coded values
decision: How to apply color, spacing, and typography values
appliesWhen: Application code defines styles using Fluent components.
notApplicableWhen: A one-off illustration or asset is not part of the component styling system.
instruction: Reference Fluent tokens through makeStyles instead of hard-coding colors, spacing, or font values, so a theme change flows through the whole app.
rationale: The token model separates global palette values from semantic aliases; hard-coded values break theming and contrast guarantees.
layoutConsequences: Token-based spacing keeps the app on one consistent rhythm with the components around it.
responsiveConsequences: Token values can change per theme and density without rewriting component styles.
accessibilityImplications: Semantic tokens carry contrast guarantees, so bypassing them can silently fail contrast.
stateImplications: Theme changes are state owned by the provider, and token-based styles react without per-component wiring.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The styling system changes how semantic tokens are referenced.

positiveExample: Component styles read `tokens.colorNeutralBackground1` and `tokens.spacingVerticalM`.
antiPattern: Writing `#ffffff` or `13px` directly into a component's style rule.
verificationMethod: A lint or review checks that application style rules reference tokens rather than literal color and spacing values.

title: Use the type ramp instead of ad-hoc font sizes
decision: How to assign text sizes and weights
appliesWhen: The interface renders text.
notApplicableWhen: The text is part of a generated image or an external embed.
instruction: Assign text a role from the Fluent type ramp and let the role determine size, weight, and line height, rather than setting font sizes per screen.
rationale: A shared ramp keeps hierarchy consistent across screens and keeps line height paired with size for readability.
layoutConsequences: Ramp-based text produces predictable line heights, so spacing between blocks stays even.
responsiveConsequences: Ramp steps may change at breakpoints without changing the semantic role of the text.
accessibilityImplications: Text must remain resizable to 200 percent and keep sufficient contrast at every ramp step.
stateImplications: None; typography is presentational.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: A new type ramp is published in a major release.

positiveExample: Page and section headings use ramp roles, and body copy uses the body role at one size.
antiPattern: Setting an 18px font size on a paragraph to make it stand out.
verificationMethod: A review confirms text styles map to ramp roles and that zoom to 200 percent does not truncate text.

title: Respect reduced motion and keep motion purposeful
decision: When and how much motion to use
appliesWhen: An interface transition or animation plays.
exceptions: Motion that conveys essential state may remain, but its duration and intensity must be reduced when the user requests less motion.
notApplicableWhen: The interface has no transitions.
instruction: Honor the user's reduced-motion preference and keep transitions short and purposeful, because motion that cannot be suppressed can cause discomfort.
rationale: Motion conveys state and hierarchy, but it must never be a barrier; the platform preference lets users opt out of non-essential movement.
layoutConsequences: Motion should not change layout; transitions animate existing surfaces rather than reflowing content.
responsiveConsequences: Animation is trimmed rather than merely sped up on low-powered or narrow devices.
accessibilityImplications: Non-essential animation must stop or reduce under the reduced-motion preference, and no content may rely on motion alone.
stateImplications: The application owns open and closed state; motion reflects it but does not gate it.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The component library changes how it consumes the reduced-motion preference.

positiveExample: Overlay transitions collapse to near-instant fades when the reduced-motion preference is set.
antiPattern: A long decorative slide-in that plays regardless of the reduced-motion setting.
verificationMethod: A test runs with the reduced-motion emulation and asserts that no long transition is applied.

title: Keep focus visible and never obscure the focused control
decision: How focus is shown during keyboard use
appliesWhen: Any interactable control can receive focus.
notApplicableWhen: A control is disabled and cannot receive focus.
instruction: Preserve a visible focus indicator on every interactive element and ensure sticky or overlaying regions never cover the focused control.
rationale: A keyboard user navigates by watching focus; if the indicator is removed or hidden behind another surface, the interface becomes unusable without a pointer.
layoutConsequences: Sticky headers and footers need scroll padding so the focused control stays in view.
responsiveConsequences: Focus remains visible when a pane collapses or a drawer opens over the page.
accessibilityImplications: Focus must be visible, contrast against adjacent colors, and the focused element must be scrolled into an unobscured area.
stateImplications: The application must move focus deliberately when content changes, rather than leaving focus on a removed element.
locators: Accessibility > Keyboard navigation and assistive technologies

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The platform changes the default focus indicator contract.

positiveExample: A skip link and scroll padding keep the focused control visible under a sticky toolbar.
antiPattern: Setting `outline: none` on a control without supplying a replacement indicator.
verificationMethod: A keyboard test tabs through the page and asserts the focused element is visible and not covered.

title: Follow the composite-widget keyboard model for grids, menus, and tabs
decision: How keyboard interaction works inside composite controls
appliesWhen: A grid, menu, tab list, or toolbar is interactive.
exceptions: A single-row action menu may use simpler keyboard handling when it is the only interactive control.
notApplicableWhen: The control is not a composite widget.
instruction: Give composite widgets a single tab stop and arrow-key movement within it, and ensure nested action controls are reachable without conflicting with row activation.
rationale: The composite model keeps the Tab sequence short while letting the arrow keys explore the widget; mixing row activation with nested controls without a plan creates conflicting handlers.
layoutConsequences: Interactive controls nested in a grid cell need enough room to be unambiguous targets.
responsiveConsequences: Keyboard behavior is unchanged at narrow widths; collapsing a region must not strand focus.
accessibilityImplications: Arrow keys, Home and End, and Escape follow the convention for the widget, and a cell containing actions must not also activate on the same key.
stateImplications: The application tracks the active cell or item separately from selection.
locators: Accessibility > Keyboard navigation and assistive technologies

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The APG changes the keyboard contract for a widget the app uses.

positiveExample: A DataGrid moves with arrow keys, and an Edit action inside a cell is reachable with Tab without activating the row.
antiPattern: A grid where every cell is a separate Tab stop, or where pressing Enter both edits and opens the row.
verificationMethod: Keyboard tests cover arrow movement, a single grid tab stop, and nested action reachability.

title: Provide names, roles, and instructions for non-text content
decision: How to make icons and controls understandable without sight
appliesWhen: An element conveys meaning through an icon, color, or shape alone.
exceptions: A purely decorative icon may be hidden from assistive technology instead of named.
notApplicableWhen: The element carries no meaning beyond the surrounding text.
instruction: Give every meaningful icon or color-coded control a programmatic name and an instruction where needed, and hide purely decorative icons from assistive technology.
rationale: Meaning that lives only in an icon or a color is unavailable to a screen reader and to users who cannot distinguish the color.
layoutConsequences: Space must be reserved for a visible text hint where color or icon is the only signal.
responsiveConsequences: A hint that is hidden at narrow widths must still be available programmatically.
accessibilityImplications: Icons used as controls require an accessible name, and status conveyed by color must also carry text or an icon with a label.
stateImplications: The application owns the text that describes a state, such as an error summary or a status label.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The component library provides naming automatically for a control.

positiveExample: A status dot is paired with a visible text label, and an icon-only button has an aria-label.
antiPattern: A red dot that means At risk with no text and no accessible name.
verificationMethod: An automated check asserts icon-only controls have accessible names and color-coded status has a text equivalent.

title: Reflow content rather than shrinking it
decision: How the layout adapts to narrow viewports and zoom
appliesWhen: The viewport narrows or the user zooms.
notApplicableWhen: The content is a fixed-format canvas such as a data visualization that provides its own alternative.
instruction: Let content reflow into a single column and scroll vertically so nothing is lost, rather than clipping or forcing two-dimensional scrolling.
rationale: Zooming and narrow screens are common; content that requires horizontal scrolling to read or that clips controls becomes inaccessible.
layoutConsequences: Multi-column regions collapse to one column, and fixed-width sidebars become overlays.
responsiveConsequences: Breakpoints are project conventions, not library mandates; each one must state the content change it triggers.
accessibilityImplications: At 400 percent zoom, content must reflow without loss of information or function and without two-dimensional scrolling.
stateImplications: Whether a pane is collapsed is application state and may reset across breakpoints.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The targeted minimum viewport changes by a documented product decision.

positiveExample: A two-column detail page becomes one column below the project's narrow breakpoint.
antiPattern: Keeping a fixed 1200px content width so the page requires horizontal scrolling at 200 percent zoom.
verificationMethod: A test renders at a narrow viewport and at 400 percent zoom and asserts no horizontal scroll and no hidden content.

title: Use logical properties so layouts mirror under RTL
decision: How to write direction-aware layout and spacing
appliesWhen: The application may be localized into a right-to-left language.
notApplicableWhen: The product is fixed to a single left-to-right locale by an explicit scope decision.
instruction: Express margins, padding, and alignment with logical properties and set the provider direction, so the layout mirrors without a separate stylesheet.
rationale: Physical properties such as left and right do not mirror, so an RTL locale would render a broken layout that must be fixed twice.
layoutConsequences: Logical spacing keeps icons and labels aligned to the reading direction.
responsiveConsequences: Mirroring is independent of viewport size and applies at every breakpoint.
accessibilityImplications: Reading order in the DOM stays the same while the visual order mirrors, so screen readers are unaffected.
stateImplications: The locale and direction are application state supplied to the provider.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The product explicitly commits to left-to-right only.

unresolved: Whether the fixture needs a full RTL pass beyond logical properties is revisited when a localization requirement is authorized.
positiveExample: Spacing uses marginInlineStart so the drawer aligns to the reading direction.
antiPattern: Padding-left values that stay on the left when the document direction is RTL.
verificationMethod: A test sets the provider direction to RTL and asserts the layout mirrors without horizontal overflow.

title: Plan for long content and truncation with an accessible full value
decision: How long labels and cell values behave
appliesWhen: A label, title, or cell may exceed its available width.
notApplicableWhen: Values have a guaranteed short format such as a date.
instruction: Let long values wrap where space allows and truncate with an accessible full value where it does not, so hidden text stays available.
rationale: Truncation without a full-value fallback hides information from everyone, and hiding it from assistive technology makes the loss invisible.
layoutConsequences: Column priorities decide what wraps and what is dropped first as width shrinks.
responsiveConsequences: Low-priority columns can be hidden behind a detail view rather than squeezed to unreadable widths.
accessibilityImplications: A truncated value needs a title or tooltip that exposes the full text, and hover-only disclosure must have a keyboard equivalent.
stateImplications: Expanding a truncated value is local state and does not change the underlying data.
locators: Microsoft Writing Style Guide > Make every word matter

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The product guarantees a maximum value length.

positiveExample: A long record name wraps in the detail view and truncates with a tooltip in the grid.
antiPattern: An ellipsized cell whose full value cannot be revealed by keyboard or pointer.
verificationMethod: A test asserts a truncated value exposes its full text through an accessible mechanism.

title: Provide one root FluentProvider with an explicit theme and direction
decision: Where theming and direction are established
appliesWhen: A Fluent UI React v9 app renders.
notApplicableWhen: The components are rendered in isolation inside an existing provider, such as a test harness.
instruction: Wrap the application in a single FluentProvider that sets the theme and text direction, and let nested providers be exceptions rather than the rule.
rationale: The provider supplies tokens and direction to every descendant; nesting providers without reason creates regions that silently ignore a theme change.
layoutConsequences: The provider establishes the token context the whole layout styles against.
responsiveConsequences: Theme and density can change per region without a second provider when token overrides are sufficient.
accessibilityImplications: Text direction must reach assistive technology so reading order matches the visual order.
stateImplications: The application owns the active theme and direction and passes them to the root provider.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The provider contract changes in a breaking release.

positiveExample: The app entry renders one FluentProvider with the chosen theme and locale direction.
antiPattern: Wrapping each screen in its own provider with a fixed light theme.
verificationMethod: check-facts confirms FluentProvider is a real export, and a test asserts the theme reaches a nested component.

title: Keep application state in the application, not in Fluent
decision: Who owns data, routing, and server state
appliesWhen: The app loads, routes, or mutates data.
notApplicableWhen: A component's internal presentational state, such as whether a menu is open, is genuinely local.
instruction: Own routing, data fetching, authorization, and persistence in application code, and use Fluent components only for presentation and local interaction state.
rationale: Fluent does not provide routing, fetching, or persistence, so assuming it does leads to designs with no owner for a required behavior.
layoutConsequences: None directly; the ownership boundary keeps data concerns out of layout code.
responsiveConsequences: None directly.
accessibilityImplications: Because the app owns updates, it also owns announcing asynchronous changes to assistive technology.
stateImplications: Server data, route state, and authorization live in application stores; component state is limited to open, focus, and draft input.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: Fluent publishes a first-party data or routing layer.

positiveExample: A route renders a detail page and the application fetches the record before handing data to the view.
antiPattern: Expecting a Nav or Dialog component to perform navigation or persistence.
verificationMethod: The fixture has an explicit data and routing module, and the skill states the boundary for each pattern.

title: Compose with makeStyles and slots instead of wrapping Fluent internals
decision: How to extend a component's look and structure
appliesWhen: A component needs custom styling or an extra internal element.
exceptions: A small wrapper is acceptable when it composes public components and adds no internal assumptions.
notApplicableWhen: The component already meets the need without customization.
instruction: Style Fluent components with makeStyles and compose their public slots, rather than depending on internal class names or undocumented DOM structure.
rationale: Internals are not part of the public contract; depending on them makes an upgrade a rewrite.
layoutConsequences: Slot composition keeps the component's own layout rules in force instead of overriding them wholesale.
responsiveConsequences: Token-driven styles adapt to breakpoints without duplicating component internals.
accessibilityImplications: Styling must not remove focus indicators or change an element's role or accessible name.
stateImplications: Custom styles should not introduce a second source of truth for component state.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The library exposes a supported extension point for the case.

positiveExample: A custom card uses makeStyles with tokens and passes content through the documented slots.
antiPattern: Overriding a generated class name such as `fui-Button__root` to change a component's padding.
verificationMethod: A review confirms custom styles reference public classes and slots and survive a patch upgrade.

title: Guard unsaved changes before they can be lost
decision: How the app protects in-progress work
appliesWhen: A form or drawer holds edits that are not yet saved.
notApplicableWhen: The surface has no editable fields.
instruction: Track dirty state and confirm before discarding unsaved changes when the user closes, navigates away from, or switches context in the editor.
rationale: Losing typed work without warning is a serious failure; a confirmation lets the user decide at the moment the risk appears.
layoutConsequences: The confirmation appears as a small dialog that does not replace the editor.
responsiveConsequences: The confirmation fits the viewport and its buttons never scroll out of reach.
accessibilityImplications: The confirmation must have a title, move focus into it, and return focus to the editor if the user cancels.
stateImplications: The application computes dirty state from the draft and the saved value and owns the pending-close state.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The product adopts autosave and removes the discard risk.

unresolved: Whether autosave is ever appropriate for the record editor is revisited if a persistence backend is authorized.
positiveExample: Closing a changed drawer opens a confirmation offering Keep editing and Discard.
antiPattern: A drawer that closes immediately and silently drops the typed values.
verificationMethod: A test edits a value, attempts to close, and asserts the confirmation appears and cancelling preserves the draft.

title: Prevent duplicate submission and show pending work
decision: How a form behaves while a submit is in flight
appliesWhen: A submit triggers an asynchronous request.
notApplicableWhen: The form saves synchronously with no request.
instruction: Disable the submit action while a request is pending, show progress in place, and re-enable the action when the request settles.
rationale: An enabled button during a pending request invites a second submission that can duplicate a record or a charge.
layoutConsequences: Reserve space for the progress indicator so the form does not shift when submission starts.
responsiveConsequences: The pending indicator remains visible at narrow widths and does not push the submit action off screen.
accessibilityImplications: A disabled pending action must remain named, and the progress state must be announced without stealing focus.
stateImplications: The application owns a submission status with at least idle, pending, succeeded, and failed values.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: A submission API guarantees idempotency and the product accepts the trade-off.

positiveExample: The Save button becomes disabled with a spinner and a Saving label until the request settles.
antiPattern: An always-enabled Save button that fires a new request on every click.
verificationMethod: A test double-clicks submit and asserts exactly one request was issued.

title: Give every sortable column a compare function
decision: How a grid column becomes sortable
appliesWhen: A grid column is presented to the user as sortable.
exceptions: A column that is intentionally not sortable needs no compare function.
notApplicableWhen: The grid has no sorting.
instruction: Provide a compare function in every column definition whose header is meant to sort; a column without compare stays unsortable even when the grid enables sorting.
rationale: The grid treats the compare function as the signal that a column can be ordered, so a sortable-looking header with no compare silently does nothing.
layoutConsequences: Sortable headers add a sort glyph and must reserve space so labels do not shift when the sort state changes.
responsiveConsequences: Keep the sort control in the header cell at narrow widths instead of moving it to a separate control that hides the current sort state.
accessibilityImplications: A sortable header exposes a sort button and the current sort state must be conveyed; because the library does not reliably announce the change, pair a sort change with a polite status message when the results update.
stateImplications: Sort state is owned by the application through sortState and onSortChange, or by the grid through defaultSortState, and compare functions must be stable.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: A first-party DataGrid usage guide specifies a different sortability signal.

positiveExample: A file list makes only name and modified-date sortable by supplying compare for those two columns.
antiPattern: Setting sortable while leaving a column definition without compare, so its header looks sortable and does nothing.
verificationMethod: A fixture sort test supplies compare for sortable columns and asserts the order or request changes.

title: Set a cell focus mode when the cell contains interactive controls
decision: How a grid cell that contains controls participates in keyboard focus
appliesWhen: A DataGrid cell or header cell contains one or more focusable controls.
exceptions: Cells with no focusable content keep the default cell behavior.
notApplicableWhen: The grid has no interactive content inside cells.
instruction: Set focusMode group on a cell with several focusable elements so Enter enters the cell and Escape returns to it, and set focusMode none on a cell with exactly one focusable element so that control receives focus directly.
rationale: The grid is a single tab stop with roving arrow keys; a cell that holds controls without an explicit focus mode either traps keyboard users or makes its controls unreachable.
layoutConsequences: Reserve room for the cell control without changing row height when the cell gains focus.
responsiveConsequences: A cell control that cannot fit collapses into an overflow menu rather than shrinking below its touch target.
accessibilityImplications: group makes the cell focusable and contains focus, while none skips the cell so the inner control is reached directly; neither may create a keyboard trap.
stateImplications: Focus stays a rendering concern; the cell does not own the control's state.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The grid changes its tab-stop and roving-focus model.

positiveExample: A cell with an Edit button and a menu sets group; a cell with a single link sets none.
antiPattern: Adding buttons inside cells with no focus mode, so arrow keys land on the cell and the buttons are unreachable.
verificationMethod: A fixture keyboard test enters an interactive cell, operates the control, and leaves with Escape.

title: Do not nest focusable controls inside a sortable header cell
decision: Where header-level actions may live in a sortable grid
appliesWhen: A sortable header cell is designed to host extra controls.
exceptions: An unsortable header cell may host controls when it sets an appropriate focus mode.
notApplicableWhen: The header cell is not sortable.
instruction: Keep a sortable header cell free of nested focusable controls; move header actions into a context menu or into the body cells instead.
rationale: A sortable header cell renders its label inside a sort button, so nesting another control creates invalid nested interaction and unpredictable keyboard behavior.
layoutConsequences: Header actions that move to a menu free the header cell to remain a single control.
responsiveConsequences: The menu keeps header actions reachable at narrow widths without widening the column.
accessibilityImplications: A sortable header cell should contain exactly one focusable element, its sort button.
stateImplications: Action state lives with the menu, not inside the header cell.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The header cell stops wrapping its label in a sort button.

positiveExample: A sortable date header stays a plain sort button; a column menu opens from a separate affordance.
antiPattern: Putting a filter button inside a sortable header cell so sorting and opening the filter interleave.
verificationMethod: A fixture test asserts a sortable header cell contains no nested focusable element.

title: Treat column resizing as a preview capability with an explicit overflow container
decision: How to place column resizing and multi-column grids
appliesWhen: The design lets users resize columns or show columns wider than the viewport.
exceptions: A grid whose columns always fit needs no resize affordance.
notApplicableWhen: The grid uses fixed, non-resizable columns.
instruction: Use resizableColumns only inside a container that allows horizontal overflow, provide the column sizing options, and keep keyboard resizing available; do not let resizing push the page into two-dimensional scrolling.
rationale: Column resizing is a preview capability; with auto-fit disabled columns can grow past the viewport, so it needs a scroll container rather than the page.
layoutConsequences: Resizing changes the grid's intrinsic width; the region scrolls, not the page.
responsiveConsequences: At narrow widths prefer hiding low-priority columns over relying on resize.
accessibilityImplications: The resize handle must be keyboard operable and named, and resizing must not obscure focus.
stateImplications: Column sizing state (columnSizingOptions and onColumnResize) is owned by the application when controlled.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: Column resizing leaves preview and its defaults change.

positiveExample: A many-column grid scrolls horizontally inside its region and lets users widen the last column.
antiPattern: Enabling resizableColumns on a full-width auto-fit grid so columns cannot be widened and the handle never appears.
verificationMethod: A fixture test resizes a column and asserts the region scrolls horizontally without page-level horizontal scroll.

title: Memoize the row render function before virtualizing a grid
decision: How to keep a virtualized grid stable
appliesWhen: The data surface is virtualized to keep large collections responsive.
exceptions: A non-virtualized grid does not need a stable renderer.
notApplicableWhen: Virtualization is not used.
instruction: Keep the row render function stable with useCallback and a stable row key before enabling virtualization, and virtualize only after measuring a performance need.
rationale: The virtualization extension builds components from the row renderer, so an inline function causes repeated unmount and mount that defeats the optimization, and virtualization also keeps only visible rows in the DOM.
layoutConsequences: Virtualized rows need a stable or measured row height for predictable scrolling.
responsiveConsequences: Preserve focus and report row position when the window of rendered rows moves.
accessibilityImplications: Expose the row position and total count, keep a stable row key, and never lose the focused element when the window shifts.
stateImplications: The application owns the virtualization harness and the stable key.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: A core virtualization API ships with the component.

positiveExample: A ten-thousand-row audit log uses a memoized renderer and a stable id key.
antiPattern: Passing an inline arrow as the row renderer to a virtualized grid.
verificationMethod: A review or example check that the virtualized row renderer is stable.

title: Give selection controls a descriptive accessible name
decision: How row-selection controls are named
appliesWhen: The grid supports row selection with selection cells.
notApplicableWhen: The grid has no selection.
instruction: Provide an aria-label through the selection cell for both the header select-all control and each row control, naming the action and, for the header, the selection scope.
rationale: Unnamed checkboxes are unusable out of context, and the header name must say whether it selects the current page or all matching results.
layoutConsequences: The label does not change the layout and must not replace the visible selection state.
responsiveConsequences: The selection cell keeps its touch target and name at narrow widths.
accessibilityImplications: Every selection checkbox needs an accessible name that states the action and, for the header, the scope.
stateImplications: The application defines the label text and the meaning of select-all.

confidence.wouldChangeIf: The selection cell supplies a default accessible name.

positiveExample: The header select-all is labelled Select all rows on this page and each row is labelled Select row <name>.
antiPattern: A grid of checkboxes with no accessible names.
verificationMethod: A fixture axe and keyboard test asserts each selection control has an accessible name that states its scope.
